items.title: GRA keeps some port interceptions quiet to protect detection methods
items.description: The Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) keeps some port discoveries out of the public domain because disclosing them could help perpetrators learn how officers detect prohibited goods, Commissioner-General Anthony Kwasi Sarpong said. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition on Thursday, he said the authority makes many discoveries that it does not announce publicly. “The more you make them public, the perpetrators learn your art of finding them,” he said. Mr Sarpong acknowledged that prohibited items sometimes pass through the ports. “Occasionally, yes, some are going through,” he said. He said the GRA works with other agencies at the ports, including narcotics officers, the Food and Drugs Board and standards agencies. Each has a specialist role, while Customs handles revenue assessment. The Authority is working towards a one-window system that would bring relevant agencies together to inspect containers. An ongoing team is also preparing a master plan to identify investment needs at ports and other border entry points, including Aflao and the airport. Mr Sarpong said the GRA uses discoveries internally to strengthen its work. He also said officers could be held accountable if they failed in their duties, and that the authority reviews what went wrong to prevent similar incidents.

items.title: I Baked My Way Through The Atlantic ’s Archives
items.description: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. The most cherished recipes are usually the hardest to follow. They live on stained index cards and notes worn thin at the creases, in handwriting so faded you have to squint to read it. That handwriting belongs to a grandmother or a distant relative, and it was meant for someone who already knew the dish: Add a pinch of this, a teacup of that; bake until done . I’ve spent a lot of time in The Atlantic ’s archives, and I kept running into such recipes tucked into letters, essays, and memoirs, rarely where you’d expect them. I was curious to know whether they still work—and, more important, how they taste. The further back I went, the less my finds looked like recipes. They read like stories, and you had to read closely to find the instructions. Take this “ Letter to a Young Housekeeper ,” from November 1865, written by C. P. Hawes to “M.,” a bride newly married to “H.” Hawes spends most of the letter arguing that cooking is a fine art and a science, which the woman of the house should learn for herself. She is funny about it, and a little grand. Recalling one early success at the table, Hawes reaches for Henry David Thoreau, whose essays had recently run in this magazine, to describe the dishes: “We ate, lingered, and revelled in them, thus becoming epicures at once … They were as great a revelation to the palate as Bettine or Thoreau might be to the mind.” Only at the very end does she mention a “well-tested” recipe for bread: a quart of milk, a teacup of “hopyeast,” and enough flour “to make it quite stiff.” How much flour? How hot an oven? And how long does it bake for? Hawes doesn’t say. For much of history, recipes moved from one cook to another by word of mouth and by experience: watching a mother at the stove, having a neighbor ask for a missing ingredient. Cookbooks didn’t exist simply because, for centuries, most women couldn’t read, Sarah Lohman, a culinary historian, told me. As literacy spread in the 18th century, women began keeping handwritten notes of family recipes to pass down or to copy for a daughter when she was married. Those recipes were light on instructions by design. They expected you to rely on your instincts “to know when the batter looks right or to know when the cake is done,” Lohman said. By the early 20th century, written recipes had become something to amass, and cookbooks were treated as literature. “It was with something of a shock that I woke one morning and found myself a collector of cookery books,” the American writer Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote in The Atlantic in 1901. What she prized most were the traces that earlier owners of the books left behind. Her copy of The Queen-Like Closet , a 17th-century cookbook by Hannah Woolley, had several owners before it reached her—one of whom was a young woman named Mary Halfpenny, who had received it as a gift in 1678 and went on to add her own recipes to its pages. A century later, another family used it as their “Bible,” recording their children’s births in the margins. Pennell loved those scribbles: “They add a distinctly personal charm to the shabby little old cookery book.” And sometimes, the actual Bible held recipes too. In 1910, a writer in this magazine’s Contributors’ Club described the family Bible as a place where you might find anything tucked between the pages, from a father’s old report cards “to mother’s recipe for sponge-cake.” But around midcentury, the American recipe changed shape, in part due to technology. I asked Lohman why some of the 19th-century recipes I’d baked didn’t call for butter or eggs. Before the advent of the refrigerator, Lohman explained, these ingredients were seasonal: Cows give milk after calving, from late winter into summer, and hens tend to take a break from laying in winter. Sure enough, the 19th-century recipes missing those ingredients were fall and winter dishes. By the mid-1950s, the majority of American homes had a refrigerator. As kitchens changed, recipes changed with them: more exact, more complete, easier for a stranger to follow. But the story behind the food has never quite gone away. Even as recipes grew more precise and the ingredients in them stopped shifting with the seasons, the people who wrote them kept reaching for memories. In 1985, Corby Kummer, then an editor at The Atlantic , began an essay on pie not with flour or butter but with a tale about his mother’s pie crust, an unforgettable taste that “has driven me to pursue the elusive art of making pastry.” And as recipes moved online, the stories came with them. Food blogs, and later videos, wrapped their instructions in anecdotes; anyone who has looked up a recipe on their phone knows the feeling of scrolling past several paragraphs of backstory before the ingredient list appears. Some of that is less sentimental than it seems (long blocks of text help a recipe rank higher in search results and make more room for ads). Still, it is telling that when food writers have space to fill, they fill it with stories. I have been baking since I was a child, learning from my mother and grandmothers and from recipes handed down for generations. I was curious whether the recipes I found from over the decades still hold up today. So I baked my way through the archives, beginning with Hawes’s 1865 biscuits and ending on a batch of brownies from 2010. Where an ingredient or instruction was missing, I filled in what I thought each recipe left out and made my best guess about certain directions (what it means to age in a tin, or to roll to “exactly the right thickness”). The recipes below are adapted from the originals, based on my own testing (I’ve indicated any discrepancies with the original recipes by adding “modified” to the ingredients list). Here’s what happened—and my honest assessment of how it all tasted. Biscuits, 1865 In C. P. Hawes’s Atlantic story , she promises her dough will make “two small loaves and a half-dozen biscuits.” What came out of my oven were plain dinner rolls, and only about a dozen (there was no dough left for the loaves). Today’s biscuits are made with butter; Hawes’s dough is mostly milk, flour, and yeast. And not the yeast we buy now. Home bakers used to make their own, often by brewing it with hops. Hawes calls for a teacup of this so-called hop yeast—I used a packet of active dry yeast instead. The result: a simple bread roll with a slightly floury taste. Not quite a Thoreau-level revelation. But if you want a very simple dinner roll for the table, this is the recipe for you. (And if you’re after a tall, fluffy biscuit, Amanda Mull cracked the code in 2018.) Apple Dowdy, 1936 The cook and writer Della T. Lutes, whose Atlantic essays became part of her award-winning 1936 book, The Country Kitchen , calls her Apple Dowdy “a homely dish,” and she wasn’t being modest. A cross between an apple pie and an apple cobbler, mine came out of the oven looking exactly as advertised. At first, I wondered whether the Dowdy came before the pie, but not quite: Sarah Lohman told me that by the end of the 18th century, pies were “pretty much how they are today.” The pandowdy is just a less fussy way to get to a similar place. Lutes gives no quantities at all—she just writes that the dish needs a deep bed of sliced, spiced, buttered apples under a thick crust, baked “at least an hour, very slowly.” The result: a slightly watery dessert that isn’t the prettiest, but tastes decent. The consistency of the filling needed improvement, and it also could have used more flavor (I’d recommend going heavier on the spice). Lebkuchen, 1949 In 1949, the cookbook author Virginia Pasley described a holiday tradition that began with a search. Her mother “tried recipe after recipe” for Lebkuchen, a spiced German honey cookie, “like Mother used to make.” The Lebkuchen that finally passed the test came from Mrs. Schmidt next door. The writer and her siblings, who wanted to help, were allowed only to sliver the almonds and cut up the citron. Now I understand why. The recipe calls for so much honey that it ended up all over my kitchen, and stirring the stiff dough with 9(!) cups of flour was an arm workout. The result: This one was divisive among my taste-testers. The Lebkuchen is dense and very chewy, a workout for your jaw too. But if you like something not too sweet or soft to dunk in tea, this could be your cookie. Apple pie, 1985 and 2009 For this one, I paired two recipes from two eras. The crust comes from Corby Kummer , who opens his 1985 essay dismissing store-bought crust as tasting “like the box it came in.” His own recipe is the opposite: flaky, rich, and well worth the effort. The filling is from Ezekiel Emanuel’s 2009 apple-crisp recipe , which was helpful enough to provide me with a list of ingredients, a pan size, and the oven temperature. Pie crust Apple crisp filling The result: Kummer’s crust was so good that it stood out to the people who tried it. (Store-bought just doesn’t compare to his recipe.) The filling was a big step up from Lutes’s Dowdy. Emanuel himself says his filling is “almost identical to the one for apple pie,” and that’s how it tasted: like a solid, classic apple pie. Overall, a satisfying combination of recipes. Brownies, 2010 The newest recipe on my list comes from my colleague Eleanor Barkhorn, a senior editor at The Atlantic . It was part of a weekly series she wrote while training for a marathon. Unlike the older recipes, it leaves almost nothing to the imagination: There are eight ingredients and exact measurements. When I reached out to Eleanor, she had a few updates to the instructions: She sometimes ups the chocolate to 10 ounces, and she no longer recommends the mixer, because it can overmix the batter. Instead, she said it’s better to sift the flour onto the batter and then fold it in carefully with a spatula. The result: very good brownies with a perfect texture that were not hard to make. They were a favorite with my tasters. Definitely worth baking a batch. PS Family recipes are still finding their way into the pages of The Atlantic . For the December issue, Danyel Smith wrote about her Aunt Louise’s famous mac and cheese and the unexpected ingredient that set it apart. Does your family have a recipe like that, with a secret, a story, and one person who makes it best? I’d love to hear about it. Let us know in the comments. (We may share your answer, including your first name and last initial, age, and/or location, with fellow readers in a future edition of this newsletter or on our website or social-media platforms.) — Rafaela

items.title: Ban sign-out ceremonies at all levels of education, say parents, student leaders
items.description: By Adesina Wahab In recent years, a fad has taken root in Nigeria’s education system, the practice of signing out of school when students conclude their examinations, even without being sure of what the results would look like. It is especially rampant at secondary school and tertiary education levels. Out of what many have labelled youthful exuberance, the graduating students do engage in various activities, including holding wild parties. In May this year, not many parents, guardians and even teachers were left bewildered when the social media was full of videos of some male secondary school students fondling their female counterparts in broad daylight. Some male students were also seen signing on the uniforms of their female colleagues in their private areas. The students were traced to a particular school in Ondo State and punishment meted out to them. But at tertiary education level, wild parties and binge drinking have led to unnecessary deaths. Only in April this year, after the second convocation ceremony of Bamidele Olumilua University of Education, Science and Technology (BOUESTI) in Ikere-Ekiti, Ekiti State, three persons, two of whom were graduating students of the university, died in a stampede that resulted from a fight at a party thrown by some students of the university. A member of staff of the hotel where the party was held was the third casualty. Investigations by the Police revealed that a fight broke out during the party and that sharp objects were freely used, leading to people scampering for safety and many people being trampled upon. Scores of people sustained varying degrees of injuries. Just few days ago, the news broke that some students of the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, died as a result of what they consumed at a sign-out party organised by some graduating students. The figure initially given was eight but in the end, four students were confirmed dead. Even if it was one person that died, human life is too valuable to be toyed with. Reacting to the development, the Governor of Enugu State, Peter Mbah, described the deaths as a grievous loss, not only to the immediate families of the deceased and the university, but also to Enugu State as a whole. He called for a ban on sign-out parties among undergraduates, noting that the practice had brought too much sorrow to families and tertiary institutions across the country. “I received with rude shock and deep sense of loss the news of the off-campus sing-out party leading to the death of four students of the University of Nigeria Nsukka, and hospitalisation of six others. “This is a grievous loss not only to the immediate families of the deceased and the university, but also to us as a state. Losing them in their prime and along with their promising future cuts as deeply as a sharp knife. We, therefore share in this grief and pray God to grant their families, friends, and the UNN community the equanimity to bear the heartbreaking loss. “Our hearts go out to their parents in particular, who sacrificed personal comforts to sponsor their children through the university, but only to face this sad turn of events. “As a government, we have ordered a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding their deaths and will work closely with the university authorities and security agencies to get to the roots of the sad development and forestall a recurrence. “Going forward, we will work with the authorities of tertiary institutions to enforce a full ban on sign-out parties and other excessive celebrations, a trend that has cost more lives and brought more sorrows than joy to families and higher institutions of learning,” the governor stated. Students go overboard at such parties — NAPTAN boss Speaking with Vanguard on the matter, the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the National Parent Teacher Association of Nigeria, Chief Adeolu Ogunbanjo, blamed excesses on the part of students for the calamities resulting from sign-out ceremonies. “Nobody is saying that people should not celebrate their accomplishments. But excess of everything is bad. Due to youthful exuberance, people do tend to go overboard during such parties. They are not like the graduation ceremonies and the attendant receptions family members organise for their children and wards. Those ones do have family members, friends and elderly people in attendance and any move to go overboard would be checked. “What should be done is that sign-out ceremonies should be banned at all levels. We cannot afford to continue losing our young ones to things we can prevent. Unfortunately, most of the time, such wild celebrations are held outside school premises, where school authorities would not have the opportunity of stopping such events. It is the duty of parents and guardians now to impress it on their wards that such events are no longer acceptable and tolerated, “ he stated. There is need for moderation — NANS Also speaking on the matter, the National Public Relations Officer of the National Association of Nigerian Students, NANS, Obidah David, said there is need for moderation in everything. “We can only sympathise with the families of the victims. We cannot hold the school authorities responsible as it happened outside the campus. What I want to say is that there is need for moderation in whatever we do. We must also be careful. Juvenile delinquencies shown by college students who would be signing and defacing their uniforms are not acceptable. Also, wild parties are not what graduating university students should engage in too. There is more to life than such things. “As student leaders, we will sensitise other students on the need to be careful. Regarding the UNN incident, there are conflicting reports on what could have been the cause of the tragic incident. At any rate, we should not put ourselves in harm’s way by our conduct. Such sign-out ceremonies must be outlawed,” he submitted. The post Ban sign-out ceremonies at all levels of education, say parents, student leaders appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: From Toronto Driveways to African Ports: Inside a $4.5 million stolen-car network
items.description: The international trade in stolen luxury vehicles has suffered a major setback after Peel Regional Police in Canada arrested 12 people and recovered 96 stolen vehicles valued at approximately $4.5 million in an extensive investigation into an alleged organised auto-theft network. The operation, code-named Project Cadetta, uncovered what investigators describe as a sophisticated criminal network involved in stealing, concealing, transporting and exporting high-value vehicles from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). According to a news release issued on November 16, 2026, Peel Regional Police laid 231 charges following an investigation launched in March 2026 in partnership with the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). At the centre of the investigation was a warehouse in Brampton, which police allege was being used as a major staging point where stolen vehicles were concealed inside shipping containers before being transported towards Canadian ports for export to West Africa. However, investigators say the operation extended well beyond the warehouse. Police allege that they uncovered a wider criminal network operating across the GTA and surrounding jurisdictions, with five key suspects responsible for coordinating the theft, movement and export of stolen vehicles. Other accused individuals allegedly played supporting roles at different stages of the operation, including loading vehicles, moving shipping containers and transporting vehicles whose identification numbers had allegedly been altered. The recovery of 96 vehicles has raised questions about how many stolen cars may have already left Canada and reached international markets before investigators could intercept them. An organised criminal supply chain beyond the driveway Project Cadetta highlights how organised vehicle theft can extend far beyond the individuals who physically steal vehicles. Investigators allege that the operation involved several layers of criminal activity, from stealing vehicles to transporting, concealing and preparing them for export. The findings are particularly concerning because stolen vehicles are not simply disappearing from residential driveways. According to police, some are allegedly being channelled into international shipping networks through organised criminal operations. Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich of Peel Regional Police described organised auto theft as a predatory business model operated by transnational criminal syndicates. He said Project Cadetta had helped dismantle the alleged supply chain, from street-level thieves to international export brokers. The 96 vehicles recovered included luxury sport utility vehicles (SUVs), pickup trucks and other high-value models. Their estimated combined value is $4.5 million. Of the 12 individuals arrested and charged, nine were released with future court dates, while three were initially held for bail hearings and subsequently released. Police also confirmed that arrest warrants had been issued for additional individuals and that further charges were anticipated as investigations continued. Ghana and Nigeria in the international auto-theft investigation For Ghanaians and Nigerians, particularly those living in Canada and those involved in the international vehicle trade, Project Cadetta carries an important cross-border dimension. Previous auto-theft investigations in the GTA have raised concerns about criminal networks allegedly shipping stolen Canadian vehicles to West African destinations, including Ghana and Nigeria. In earlier investigations, York Regional Police uncovered alleged networks involving vehicle thieves, traffickers and individuals responsible for loading stolen vehicles into shipping containers for export. One such operation, Project Victory, resulted in the recovery of 70 stolen vehicles valued at approximately $4.5 million. Police also linked the alleged network to 32 stolen vehicles that had been shipped to Ghana or Nigeria. Another investigation, Project Majestic, focused on the theft of Lexus, Toyota and Honda SUVs. These investigations demonstrate why Canadian authorities are increasingly treating organised auto theft as a cross-border and international criminal activity rather than simply a local property offence. However, the nationalities of those arrested in Project Cadetta have not been established in the police announcement. It would therefore be inaccurate to associate the accused with any particular nationality without confirmation from investigators or court records. Similarly, the recovery of vehicles allegedly destined for overseas markets does not mean that every person purchasing a luxury vehicle in Ghana or Nigeria is connected to criminal activity. Nevertheless, the investigations raise important questions for international vehicle buyers, shipping companies, vehicle dealers and port authorities about the movement and resale of stolen vehicles across borders. What happens to vehicles already shipped overseas? One of the major questions emerging from these investigations concerns vehicles that may have left Canada before police could identify and recover them. In previous investigations in the GTA, police reported that stolen vehicles were transported to the Port of Montreal, sometimes by road and sometimes in shipping containers moved by rail, before being loaded onto vessels bound for overseas destinations. This presents a significant challenge for Canadian and international authorities: identifying and recovering stolen vehicles after they have crossed international borders. The CBSA’s involvement in Project Cadetta highlights the importance of intelligence-sharing and coordinated inspections of shipping containers. Acting Regional Director General Trishann Pascal said CBSA officers play a critical role in preventing stolen vehicles from reaching international markets through targeted container examinations and referrals. For prospective buyers in Ghana and Nigeria, the investigations also underline the importance of conducting proper checks before purchasing imported vehicles. A luxury vehicle offered at an unusually attractive price should not automatically be considered a bargain. Buyers are advised to verify its documentation, ownership history and vehicle identification number (VIN) before completing a transaction. A vehicle that appears to be legally registered in one country could still be linked to an unresolved theft investigation in another. The fight against organised auto theft continues Peel Regional Police report that auto thefts across the region have declined by more than 50 per cent since reaching a peak in 2023, with a further 10 per cent year-to-date reduction recorded in 2026. While the figures indicate progress, Project Cadetta demonstrates that investigators continue to face organised criminal networks capable of operating across municipal, provincial and international boundaries. The next challenge will be determining whether the latest arrests will lead investigators to additional suspects, overseas buyers, shipping intermediaries and other individuals allegedly involved in the criminal supply chain. For the owners whose vehicles have been stolen, recovering them represents more than a financial victory. It is also about restoring a sense of security, protecting livelihoods and ensuring that criminal networks cannot turn ordinary Canadian neighbourhoods into starting points for international illegal trade. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Peel Regional Police Commercial Auto Crime Bureau on 905-453-2121, extension 3410. One thing is clear: the fight against organised auto theft cannot end at Canada’s borders. If stolen vehicles are being moved across oceans, the response must extend across borders as well.

items.title: We must never forget this man
items.description: Inspector Issa Kanjarga: The Ghanaian Police Officer Who Defied A Colonial Order And Helped Prevent A Massacre On 28 February 1948. Imagine standing in front of a crowd of unarmed men, knowing that your superior has ordered you to open fire. You are wearing the same uniform, carrying the same weapon, and serving under the same colonial authority. But at that moment, you must make a decision: obey the order or save lives. On February 28, 1948, at Christiansborg Castle in Accra, a Gold Coast police officer reportedly made a decision that would put him on the wrong side of his colonial superiors but earn him a place in Ghana’s history. His name was Inspector Issa Kanjarga. He defined his superior, and screamed in an indigenous language that his colleagues should not obey orders to fire on their own compatriots.

items.title: Brahim Diaz aurait prolongé au Real Madrid, mais réclamerait davantage de temps de jeu
items.description: Le dossier contractuel de Brahim Diaz aurait connu une issue favorable. D’après le journaliste Matteo Moretto, l’international marocain aurait déjà signé sa prolongation avec le Real Madrid. Mais si son avenir contractuel semble désormais sécurisé, son statut sportif reste, lui, incertain. Arrivé à un moment charnière de sa carrière, Brahim Diaz aurait finalement choisi de poursuivre son aventure avec le Real Madrid. Selon les informations de Matteo Moretto, le joueur de 27 ans a déjà signé son nouveau contrat avec le club madrilène, à l’instar de Thibaut Courtois. Cette prolongation interviendrait alors que l’avenir de l’international marocain faisait l’objet de nombreuses interrogations. Son précédent contrat courait jusqu’en juin 2027 et plusieurs informations évoquaient ces derniers mois une possible prolongation jusqu’en 2030. Le Real Madrid n’a toutefois pas encore officialisé les détails du nouvel accord. Si la question contractuelle semblerait désormais réglée, Brahim Diaz doit encore obtenir davantage de garanties sur le plan sportif. Depuis le début de la saison 2026/27, l’attaquant peine à s’imposer dans les plans de José Mourinho. Le Marocain compte actuellement 249 minutes en neuf rencontres officielles, avec trois passes décisives et aucun but en Liga et en Ligue des champions, selon les statistiques disponibles. En championnat, il n’a disputé que 149 minutes réparties sur six apparitions. Son temps de jeu est légèrement plus important en Ligue des champions, où il a participé à trois rencontres et délivré ses trois passes décisives. Un bilan qui témoigne néanmoins d'un rôle encore secondaire dans la rotation madrilène. La prolongation de contrat ne signifierait donc pas que Brahim Diaz accepte son statut actuel. D’après Matteo Moretto, le joueur souhaite surtout augmenter son temps de jeu au fil de la saison. La concurrence reste particulièrement forte dans le secteur offensif du Real Madrid. Vinícius Junior, Arda Güler ou encore Yan Diomande figurent parmi les joueurs susceptibles de passer devant lui dans la hiérarchie établie par José Mourinho. Pour Brahim, l’enjeu sera désormais de profiter de chaque opportunité afin de convaincre son entraîneur et de gagner progressivement une place plus importante dans le onze madrilène. The post Brahim Diaz aurait prolongé au Real Madrid, mais réclamerait davantage de temps de jeu appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Ecuador: ENOS - Lluvia e inundaciones - Flash Update No. 02 (al 17 de noviembre 2026)
items.description: Country: Ecuador Source: UN Country Team in Ecuador Please refer to the attached file. DESTACADOS Según cifras oficiales, desde el 29 de agosto de 2026, las lluvias asociadas al fenómeno de El Niño han dejado más de 80.000 personas impactadas y afectaciones a 166 cantones y 508 parroquias, con predominio de inundaciones (57%) y deslizamientos (17%). Los pronósticos del Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN) y del Centro Internacional para la Investigación del Fenómeno de El Niño (CIIFEN) indican que El Niño continúa fortaleciéndose y podría alcanzar una intensidad fuerte a muy fuerte entre finales de 2026 e inicios de 2027, aumentando el riesgo de lluvias intensas, inundaciones y crecidas de ríos, particularmente en la región Costa. Las evaluaciones preliminares realizadas en territorios afectados identifican necesidades prioritarias en alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene, salud, seguridad alimentaria, protección y recuperación temprana, especialmente entre hogares que han sufrido daños en sus viviendas y pérdida de bienes esenciales. El Gobierno mantiene la Alerta Roja nacional por el fenómeno de El Niño y coordina la respuesta a través de 215 Comités de Operaciones de Emergencias (en adelante COE) activos, mientras que la asistencia humanitaria entregada supera los 60.000 bienes de ayuda distribuidos por la SNGR y las instituciones del Sistema Nacional Descentralizado de Gestión Integral de Riesgos y Desastres (en adelante SNDGIRD).(34.130 por La Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos- SNGR y 26.794 por el SNDGIRD). RESUMEN DE LA SITUACIÓN Las lluvias asociadas al fortalecimiento del fenómeno de El Niño continúan generando afectaciones en Ecuador. Desde el 29 de agosto hasta el 17 de noviembre de 2026, según cifras oficiales, se han registrado al menos 83.975 personas impactadas (51.095 afectadas y 32.880 damnificadas), además, se reportan 1.500 eventos adversos relacionados con precipitaciones en las 24 provincias, afectando a 166 cantones y 508 parroquias. Las inundaciones representan el 57% de los eventos reportados, seguidas por deslizamientos (17%), lluvias intensas (7%) y vendavales (6%). Las provincias con mayor impacto en la población son Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Los Ríos, Santa Elena, Manabí, Galápagos y Bolívar. De acuerdo con el Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN), las condiciones oceánicas y atmosféricas continúan mostrando el fortalecimiento del evento, con una probabilidad superior al 83% de que alcance una intensidad fuerte a muy fuerte durante los próximos meses. Este escenario coincide con los análisis del Centro Internacional para la Investigación del Fenómeno de El Niño (CIIFEN), que identifica el periodo entre octubre y diciembre de 2026 como la fase de mayor intensidad del fenómeno, aumentando el riesgo de lluvias por encima de lo normal, inundaciones y crecidas de ríos en la región Costa. En respuesta al incremento de las afectaciones, las autoridades nacionales y locales han fortalecido las acciones de preparación y respuesta, incluyendo la activación de mecanismos de coordinación de emergencia, la emisión de alertas y declaratorias correspondientes, así como la movilización de asistencia humanitaria para las poblaciones afectadas. De manera paralela, las instituciones del sistema nacional de gestión de riesgos mantienen el monitoreo de las condiciones hidrometeorológicas y de la evolución del fenómeno de El Niño, con el fin de anticipar impactos y ampliar las capacidades de respuesta en los territorios de mayor exposición.

items.title: 62 nouveaux candidats interpellés à Kafountine
items.description: Ils ne désespèrent toujours pas. Malgré les nombreux échecs des tentatives qui se suivent presque partout dans le pays, les candidats à la migration irrégulière continuent de tenter cette aventure périlleuse. Dans la nuit du 18 au 19 novembre, 62 nouveaux candidats ont été interpellés à Kafountine par la brigade de proximité de la localité. Il s’agit de 44 sénégalais dont 42 hommes, une femme, une mineure de 12 ans seulement et de 13 gambiens dont 8 femmes, 5 hommes dont un mineur de 9 ans seulement, et enfin de 5 guinéens tous des hommes. « Suite à un renseignement faisant état d’un probable départ au bolong de Etinpack dans la commune de Kafountine, un transport a été effectué sur les lieux où dispersés par petits groupes, ils ont été appréhendés et regroupés entre 5 heures et 8 heures », détaille une source sécuritaire. Les candidats parmi lesquels il y a d’éventuels passeurs ont été conduits à la brigade de proximité pour identification. Depuis presqu’une semaine, la brigade de proximité de Kafountine et la brigade territoriale de Diouloulou mènent des opérations de recherche, d’interception et d’interpellation de candidats et surtout des meneurs notamment les organisateurs, convoyeurs, facilitateurs, passeurs et logeurs dans le secteur de Kataba 1, Abéné, Dianah, Niafrang, les bolongs des îles Karone. items.title: Siguiri : ce que Thomas Sankara nous aurait dit (Par Mohamed Bangoura)
items.description: En suspendant l'orpaillage artisanal dans la région de Siguiri, la Guinée a fait un choix difficile mais nécessaire : protéger ses fleuves, ses forêts et ses terres, patrimoine des générations futures. Ce choix a suscité des remous chez nos voisins. Il doit pourtant être compris pour ce qu'il est : un acte de souveraineté écologique, que ni Thomas Sankara ni Ahmed Sékou Touré n'auraient renié. Une décision de survie, pas de rejet Le 2 novembre 2026, le gouvernement guinéen a interdit l'exploitation anarchique de l'or dans la région de Siguiri : dans le lit des cours d'eau, les forêts classées et les espaces protégés. Ce qui a été interdit, ce n'est pas la présence de nos voisins. C'est un mode d'exploitation qui éventre les berges, rase les forêts et empoisonne les eaux au cyanure et au mercure. Aucun État digne de ce nom ne peut regarder son territoire mourir et appeler cela de l'hospitalité. La preuve que cette décision ne vise pas les étrangers : la Guinée a commencé par sanctionner les siens. Le 16 novembre, la CRIEF a condamné l'ancien gouverneur, d'anciens préfets et sous-préfets de Siguiri à deux ans de prison ferme pour complicité de dégradation de l'environnement, et plus de 400 présidents de districts sont annoncés devant la justice. Un État qui juge ses propres serviteurs ne mène pas une chasse à l'étranger : il rétablit la loi pour tous. Du Niger à Sankara, une écologie sans frontière Siguiri se trouve à la confluence du Niger et du Tinkisso. Le fleuve naît sur notre sol avant d'arroser le Mali, le Niger et le Nigeria : chaque gramme de mercure versé à Siguiri descend vers Bamako et Niamey. Protéger le Niger à sa source n'est pas un geste nationaliste, c'est un service rendu à tout le Sahel. Et l'on ne peut revendiquer la maîtrise de son sol à Ouagadougou tout en contestant ce même droit à Conakry. En avril 1985, bien avant que l'on parle de « transition écologique », le gouvernement de Thomas Sankara lançait les « Trois luttes » : contre les feux de brousse, la divagation des animaux et la coupe abusive du bois, devenus des infractions passibles d'amendes et de prison. Le 5 février 1986, à Paris, il lançait : « L'impérialisme est le pyromane de nos forêts et de nos savanes. » Pour lui, défendre l'arbre, c'était défendre la souveraineté africaine. Que dirait Sankara devant les berges éventrées de Siguiri ? Il ne demanderait pas pourquoi la Guinée a fermé les sites, mais pourquoi elle a attendu si longtemps. Se réclamer de lui pour défendre l'orpaillage sauvage, c'est trahir sa pensée. Sékou Touré : un panafricanisme de dignité, pas de complaisance La Guinée n'a de leçon de panafricanisme à recevoir de personne. Le 25 août 1958, face au général de Gaulle, Ahmed Sékou Touré lançait : « Nous préférons la pauvreté dans la liberté à la richesse dans l'esclavage. » Un mois plus tard, notre peuple votait non, et la Guinée proclamait son indépendance le 2 octobre 1958, seule colonie de l'Afrique française à oser ce choix. Mais le panafricanisme de Sékou Touré n'a jamais été un renoncement à la souveraineté : c'était l'alliance de peuples libres et maîtres de leur sol. La phrase de 1958 résonne aujourd'hui à Siguiri : mieux vaut renoncer à un or extrait dans le désordre que d'hypothéquer la terre, l'eau et la dignité de la nation. Défendre son territoire n'est pas trahir l'Afrique ; c'est la condition même d'une unité entre égaux. « On veille au respect des règles et au respect de notre pays », le Président Mamadi Doumbouya Le 11 novembre, en marge du Simandou Mining Summit, le président Mamadi Doumbouya a fixé la ligne : « On a été un peu indulgent par notre panafricanisme, mais à partir de maintenant, on veille au respect des règles et au respect de notre pays. Et ça, nous n'avons ni amis ni parents. ». Ces mots viennent d'un chef d'État qui a refusé que la Guinée s'associe aux sanctions de la CEDEAO contre le Mali, au nom de la solidarité avec un pays frère. La Guinée a prouvé sa fraternité quand elle coûtait cher et quand il fallait être courageusement panafricain pour l'afficher ; elle a aujourd'hui le droit d'exiger qu'on respecte ses lois. La Présidence de la République l'a résumé dans son éditorial du 18 novembre 2026 : la Guinée « choisit l'action pour défendre sa souveraineté, protéger ses ressources et restaurer l'autorité de l'État », car « le leadership ne se mesure pas au bruit des plateaux télévisés, mais au courage des décisions ». La protection de l'environnement ne peut être sacrifiée au nom de la fraternité africaine. La fraternité véritable ne consiste pas à fermer les yeux sur ce qui détruit la maison commune. Ce système a aussi ses victimes. Parmi les personnes poursuivies figurent des responsables de traite des êtres humains : derrière l'or clandestin, des travailleurs vulnérables et des familles, parfois avec leurs enfants, sont livrés à des réseaux qui les exploitent. Les démanteler protège aussi les ressortissants du Burkina Faso et du Mali. On objectera que l'État ménage les sociétés minières. C'est faux : audits du secteur, dizaines de permis révoqués et, depuis juin 2026, interdiction d'exporter l'or brut. L'exigence vaut pour tous, et devra s'appliquer avec la même fermeté à la restauration des sites industriels. Ce que nous devons aux générations futures Pensons d'abord aux Guinéens de Siguiri. Des milliers de familles de Haute-Guinée vivent de l'orpaillage depuis des générations : c'est une tradition séculaire, pas seulement une activité clandestine. La suspension frappe durement l'économie locale. Protéger la terre ne doit pas signifier abandonner ceux qui en vivent : l'État doit leur ouvrir rapidement des sites encadrés, un accès au crédit et des chemins de reconversion vers l'agriculture et la transformation locale de l'or. Le Gouvernement en a conscience. Depuis 2022, avec le Forum des Mines et du Développement Durable, (FOMIDE), nous réunissons l'État, les sociétés minières et la société civile autour d'une conviction simple : l'or, la bauxite et les multiples richesses du sous-sol guinéen ne valent rien sur une terre morte. J'ai entendu, édition après édition, les mêmes promesses de mines responsables. Siguiri montre ce qu'il en coûte quand on les oublie, et ce que l'on gagne quand un État décide enfin de les tenir. Je viens de boucler une mission de travail dans les quatre régions naturelles de la Guinée. Nzérékoré à Boké, en passant par Kankan et Labé, notre vrai trésor n'est pas sous nos pieds. C'est notre biodiversité, cette nature qui change de visage d'une région à l'autre, d'une saison à l'autre. L'or de Siguiri finira par s'épuiser ; le Niger, lui, doit couler encore pour nos enfants et pour ceux de Bamako, de Ouagadougou et de Niamey. Personne n'a le droit de priver les générations futures de ce trésor. C'est cela, au fond, l'héritage de Sankara et de Sékou Touré : une Afrique libre, sur une terre encore vivante. C'est cet héritage que préserve aujourd'hui le président Mamadi Doumbouya. Les remerciements et félicitations viendront du futur. Mohamed BANGOURA , président du Comité d'organisation du Forum des Mines et du Développement Durable (FOMIDE), Directeur général de l'Office Guinéen de Publicité. items.title: Goldfields wins overall CSR company at Ghana Club 100
items.description: Mining giant Goldfields Ghana Limited emerged as the overall winner in the Corporate Social Responsibility category at the 22nd Ghana Club 100 Awards in Accra. The company was also ranked in the top three on the Club 100 rankings, following MTN Ghana and Newmont, respectively. The Ghana Investment Promotion Authority held the 22nd edition of the Ghana Club 100 Awards to recognize top-performing companies contributing to economic growth and demonstrating exemplary business leadership. Speaking to JoyBusiness, Senior Vice President of Goldfields, Elliot Williams, said the award is a testament to the CSR initiatives by the company and encourages them to do more for the host communities and the people of Ghana. “We have been doing corporate social responsibility long before it was recognized in the rankings, and for us, we always want to give back to our communities and improve the living conditions of our people—not just for the awards, but for a positive impact in their lives. We have a positive outlook, and we can assure you that more will be coming in our CSR journey,” he said. After presenting awards to the top three companies, President John Dramani Mahama urged indigenous businesses to identify opportunities within the government’s $10 billion New Economy Programme and position themselves to benefit. Chief Executive of the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority, Simon Madjie, said the agency remains committed to supporting businesses by facilitating investment and addressing challenges in the business environment. The theme for the 22nd Ghana Club 100 Awards is “Investing in Ghana’s New Economy—Building a Productive Economy That Creates Value and Competes Globally.”

items.title: Diplomatie sécuritaire : le Maroc multiplie les partenariats
items.description: Ces dernières années, les accords sécuritaires conclus par le directeur général de la Direction générale de la Sûreté nationale (DGSN) et directeur général de la Direction générale de la Surveillance du territoire (DGST), Abdellatif Hammouchi, avec des partenaires internationaux se sont multipliés, dans divers domaines liés à la sécurité et au renseignement. De l’Éthiopie au Brésil, du Liberia aux Émirats arabes unis, de Rabat à Stockholm, Oslo, Amsterdam, Paris et Madrid… les partenariats sécuritaires marocains ne cessent de se diversifier et de se multiplier, ouvrant de larges perspectives pour faire valoir le modèle sécuritaire marocain comme partenaire dans l’édification de la sécurité et l’instauration de la stabilité mondiale. Mémorandums d’entente et partenariats transnationaux Au début de cette semaine, Abdellatif Hammouchi a signé un mémorandum d’entente bilatéral avec le Commandement général de la police de Dubaï, qui a posé les bases d’un partenariat transversal et durable dans les différents domaines liés à la sécurité et à la coopération policière. Avant ce nouveau mémorandum, le directeur général de la Sûreté nationale avait ouvert la voie à l’investissement dans la formation policière et le renforcement des capacités des ressources humaines avec les Émirats arabes unis, à travers un mémorandum d’entente bilatéral avec le Commandement général de la police d’Abou Dhabi, qui a fourni l’assise juridique et organisationnelle d’une coopération durable dans les domaines de l’entraînement, de la formation et de la qualification du capital humain policier. Cette coopération bilatérale avec les Émirats arabes unis n’a été ni une exception ni une étape isolée d’une stratégie intégrée et de long terme adoptée par Abdellatif Hammouchi, selon une vision ambitieuse fondée sur la diversification des partenariats sécuritaires, la consolidation des engagements avec les pays frères et amis, ainsi que l’ouverture à de nouveaux partenaires internationaux aux quatre coins du monde, au service des intérêts supérieurs du Royaume du Maroc sous l’angle de la diplomatie sécuritaire. Ce qui frappe dans ces engagements conventionnels conclus par le directeur général de la Sûreté nationale et de la Surveillance du territoire, c’est la diversité de leurs formes de coopération et de leur étendue géographique. Le partenariat conclu avec le Commandement général de la police de Dubaï vise la coopération sécuritaire et en matière de renseignement dans la lutte contre les différentes formes de criminalité, ainsi que l’échange d’expériences et le partage des meilleures pratiques en matière de sécurité des frontières, tandis que le mémorandum d’entente signé avec le Commandement général de la police d’Abou Dhabi prévoyait d’investir dans la formation policière et le renforcement des capacités humaines. Sur le plan de l’étendue géographique, les mémorandums d’entente signés par les services de sûreté marocains sous la direction de Hammouchi ont gagné des pays et des continents géographiquement éloignés. En mai 2024, un mémorandum d’entente de coopération sécuritaire a été signé avec la Police fédérale brésilienne. Sur le continent africain, un mémorandum similaire a ensuite été signé avec la Police fédérale éthiopienne le 24 novembre 2025 à Marrakech, en marge de la 93e Assemblée générale d’Interpol, puis un autre avec la Police nationale du Liberia, en mai 2026 à Rabat, lors de la 7e édition des Journées portes ouvertes de la DGSN. Europe du Nord : un partenariat inédit La diplomatie sécuritaire marocaine lancée par Abdellatif Hammouchi a ouvert une nouvelle fenêtre dans les pays d’Europe du Nord, notamment en Scandinavie. Les premiers accords ont été conclus avec la Norvège en novembre 2025, en marge des travaux de l’Assemblée générale de l’Organisation internationale de police criminelle (Interpol), accueillie par la ville ocre, Marrakech. Dans le prolongement de cette orientation, Abdellatif Hammouchi a conclu un mémorandum d’entente similaire avec la Police nationale suédoise en avril 2026, lors de la visite de travail qu’il a effectuée à Stockholm. Ce mémorandum bilatéral a constitué un socle conventionnel solide, qui a contribué à rapprocher les points de vue entre la police marocaine et son homologue suédoise et à coordonner leurs efforts au sein d’un partenariat sécuritaire, lequel a abouti à l’arrestation de plusieurs personnes recherchées par la justice suédoise dans des affaires de criminalité organisée transnationale. Ce partenariat maroco-suédois, né du mémorandum d’entente bilatéral conclu par Abdellatif Hammouchi, a été largement salué au sein du gouvernement suédois et de ses différents services de sécurité, qui ne cessent de saluer hautement le rôle des services de sûreté marocains dans la traque des personnes recherchées à l’échelle internationale et dans leur privation de toute base arrière et de tout refuge sûr. Dans un périmètre géographique voisin, la Direction générale de la Sûreté nationale, représentée par la préfecture de police de Tanger, et la Police nationale néerlandaise, représentée par l’Unité de police du Centre des Pays-Bas, ont signé le jeudi 12 novembre courant une « lettre d’intention », nouvel instrument conventionnel destiné à établir un cadre durable de coopération bilatérale et à consolider le partenariat professionnel entre les deux institutions par l’échange d’expériences, de connaissances et de meilleures pratiques en matière de sécurité. Quant à la France, partenaire habituel, Abdellatif Hammouchi avait déjà signé, le 24 juin 2025 à Rabat, avec son homologue français, le directeur général de la Police nationale française, Louis Laugier, un plan d’action conjoint, dans une démarche commune visant à hisser la coopération sécuritaire maroco-française au niveau des relations stratégiques entre les deux pays. Ce partenariat privilégié a permis, en une seule semaine, à la mi-novembre courant, l’arrestation de quatre personnes recherchées par la justice française dans des affaires d’homicide volontaire, de constitution de bande criminelle et de règlements de comptes entre réseaux du crime organisé. La multiplication et l’accroissement de ces accords et engagements sécuritaires, la pluralité de leurs acteurs et leur ouverture à de nouveaux partenaires en dehors des partenariats classiques sont de nature à servir l’image du Maroc et à renforcer sa présence sécuritaire aux niveaux régional et international, comme à consolider les efforts internationaux de lutte contre les différentes formes de criminalité transnationale. items.title: Ghanaian among 21 arrested in Canada over alleged towing industry crime network
items.description: A Ghanaian is among 21 people arrested and charged in Canada following a major police investigation into alleged organised crime, violence and criminal activities within the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) towing industry. The investigation, code-named Project Swords, has resulted in 112 criminal charges and exposed what police describe as an alleged criminal network involved in murder conspiracies, firearms trafficking, vehicle theft, arson, fraud and other serious offences. The Ghanaian, identified as Foster Nyarko, 34, of Vaughan, was among those named in a November 18, 2026, announcement by the Toronto Police Service. The investigation was conducted in partnership with York Regional Police, Durham Regional Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police. It culminated on November 12, when officers carried out coordinated enforcement operations, arrested several suspects and executed search warrants across the GTA. Police allege that the organisation was led by Manoharan (Mano) Subramaniam, 43, of Whitby, who is accused of directing a conspiracy to murder two individuals connected to the towing industry. Investigators say three individuals were arrested before the planned killings could be carried out and have been charged with conspiracy to commit murder. The investigation points to an alleged escalation in competition for control of the towing business, an industry that provides essential roadside assistance but has increasingly become associated with violence and criminal activities, according to police. How towing industry disputes escalated into violence Police say the GTA experienced a significant increase in violence involving competing groups seeking control of the towing industry from early 2023. The reported incidents included homicides, shootings, arson, intimidation and extortion. One of the most alarming incidents was a mass shooting at a pub in Scarborough in March 2025, which left 12 people injured. The scale of the violence is also reflected in Toronto’s shooting statistics. Police reported that 62 shooting and firearm-discharge incidents in 2024 were connected to tow-truck disputes, representing nearly 13 per cent of all such incidents in the city. The figure declined to 18 incidents in 2025, representing seven per cent, and fell further to five incidents in 2026 up to the date of the announcement. Police attribute the reduction partly to coordinated investigations targeting competing criminal organisations. Project Swords follows Project Yankee, an earlier investigation targeting another faction known as “The Union”. Together, the two operations focused on what investigators described as the two largest competing groups associated with violence in the GTA towing industry. The 21 accused named by police The Toronto Police Service identified the following 21 individuals as having been arrested and charged in connection with Project Swords: Dinesh Battula, 38 , of Toronto. Fedrol Bryan, 41 , of Toronto. Harithas Gnanalingam, 48 , of Beaverton. Vathsuthan Gobalakirishnan, 41 , of Whitchurch-Stouffville. Mohamad-Ali Hamam, 29 , of Toronto. Dogan Kruezi, 29 , of Toronto. Foster Nyarko, 34 , of Vaughan. Shiv Patel, 31 , of Toronto. Ratnakumar Pirakalathan, 46 , of Toronto. Suman Pushparajah, 45 , of Toronto. Nirjan Raguthas, 25 , of Markham. Sivanesan Rajendram, 50 , of Keswick. Sadeed Rehman, 28 , of Oshawa. Kokul Senthilvel, 32 , of Toronto. Piratwipan Sivakumaran, 34 , of Pickering. Manoharan Subramaniam, 43 , of Whitby. Thanugopithan Sugumarasungam, 30 , of Toronto. Thanaraj Thangarajah, 39 , of Toronto. Jeyanan Thangavadivel, 41 , of Whitby. Kiranpal Toor, 26 , of Caledon. Kranthi Vasireddy, 37 , of Toronto. The charges outlined in the police announcement include conspiracy to commit murder, participation in a criminal organisation, firearms trafficking, possession of stolen property for trafficking, altering vehicle identification numbers, conspiracy to commit arson, fraud and breach of trust. Subramaniam faces two counts of conspiracy to commit murder, as well as charges of assault, uttering threats and conspiracy related to fraud. Nyarko and Sadeed Rehman face several charges connected to their alleged participation in a criminal organisation involved in trafficking stolen vehicles, possessing property obtained through crime and altering vehicle identification numbers. Mohamad-Ali Hamam also faces multiple charges relating to alleged participation in a criminal organisation, stolen-vehicle trafficking and attempts to alter vehicle identification numbers. The police announcement further identifies firearms-trafficking allegations involving several accused, including Shiv Patel, Kokul Senthilvel, Thanugopithan Sugumarasungam and Thanaraj Thangarajah. Piratwipan Sivakumaran, who is identified as a correctional employee, has been charged with breach of trust. Investigation uncovers alleged criminal activities beyond towing The investigation reportedly uncovered criminal activities extending beyond disputes over roadside assistance contracts. Police said officers seized several firearms, including a converted fully automatic firearm, 84 rounds of ammunition and approximately 250 grams of cocaine. According to investigators, six arrests were linked to an alleged organised vehicle-theft operation, two to an arson investigation, three to fraudulent physiotherapy clinics and one to an alleged breach of trust involving a correctional employee. Investigators also allege that Subramaniam exercised control over businesses and their finances, even where some associated properties and businesses were registered in the names of other individuals. The businesses identified included Williams Towing and Bob’s Towing. Following the enforcement operation, the Toronto Police Service immediately terminated its contractual relationship with Williams Towing, which had provided contracted services in four police divisions. Temporary service providers have since been engaged while the police service makes arrangements for a longer-term procurement process. Police outline next steps Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw credited cooperation among the participating police services and government partners for the outcome of the investigation. The Ontario government’s Ministry of the Solicitor General provided funding for the operation, with additional support from Criminal Intelligence Service Ontario. Although police have described Project Swords as a significant disruption of organised crime, the investigation has also drawn attention to concerns about how criminal networks allegedly penetrate legitimate businesses and exploit essential services. For residents and legitimate towing operators, the concern extends beyond competition for business contracts to whether the industry can operate without threats, intimidation and violence. The 21 accused are expected to face criminal proceedings, but the allegations against them have yet to be tested in court. They are all presumed innocent until proven guilty. Police are appealing to anyone with information about the investigation to contact the Toronto Police Service on 416-808-2510 . As the GTA continues to grapple with the consequences of years of alleged violence within its towing industry, Project Swords marks another significant phase in efforts to establish the full extent of the criminal networks and identify the individuals and businesses allegedly connected to their activities.

items.title: Tentative d’évasion à Ouagadougou : un garde aspergé de poudre dans les yeux par un prisonnier
items.description: Courant la fin du mois d’octobre 2026, Zoodomail.bf a appris une tentative d’évasion survenue dans le milieu carcéral de Ouagadougou. Un détenu, qui aurait tenté de prendre la fuite lors d’une évacuation sanitaire dans un établissement hospitalier. Que s’est-il passé ? Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction de Zoodomail.bf, les faits se seraient déroulés à la suite d’un problème de santé signalé par un détenu incarcéré à la MACO. Condamné à une lourde peine, ce dernier aurait informé le dispensaire de la prison que son état de santé nécessitait une prise en charge dans un établissement hospitalier. Après les premières vérifications, une autorisation lui aurait été accordée pour se rendre dans un hôpital de la place afin d’y subir des examens médicaux et de recevoir les soins nécessaires. Pour ce déplacement, le détenu était accompagné des gardes pénitentiaires chargés d'assurer sa surveillance et son assistance durant la prise en charge médicale. Mais une fois à l’hôpital, la situation aurait pris une tournure inattendue. Alors que l’un des gardes assistait le détenu à l’intérieur de la salle de soins, ce dernier aurait sorti de la poudre qu’il aurait projetée dans les yeux de son accompagnateur, selon une source de Zoodomail.bf. Profitant de la désorientation du garde, il aurait alors tenté de prendre la fuite. Cependant, son projet n'aurait pas abouti. Le deuxième garde pénitentiaire, qui était armé et se trouvait à proximité, aurait réagi à la tentative d’évasion. Il aurait fait usage de son arme à feu, atteignant le détenu par balle et mettant ainsi fin à sa course. Alerte sociale Cet incident remet en lumière les risques auxquels les gardes pénitentiaires peuvent être exposés dans l’exercice de leurs fonctions, particulièrement lors des déplacements de détenus en dehors des établissements carcéraux. Les évacuations sanitaires, les audiences judiciaires et les autres sorties autorisées constituent des moments qui nécessitent une vigilance particulière. Les agents chargés de l’escorte doivent en effet assurer à la fois l’assistance des détenus et la sécurité de leur prise en charge. Une situation comme celle-ci rappelle également l’importance des mesures de sécurité adaptées, de la coordination entre les agents et de leur préparation face aux éventuelles tentatives de fuite ou aux comportements imprévisibles. La protection des gardes pénitentiaires est aussi un enjeu de sécurité publique. Elle doit permettre aux agents d’accomplir leurs missions dans des conditions sécurisées, tout en garantissant le respect de l’intégrité physique et des droits des personnes détenues. Par Ibrahim Cissé | Zoodomail.bf L’article Tentative d’évasion à Ouagadougou : un garde aspergé de poudre dans les yeux par un prisonnier est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Canada Police extend authority to publish image of 17-year-old suspect in murder of Ghanaian teen
items.description: Toronto Police have secured an extension of judicial authorisation to publicly identify a 17-year-old suspect wanted in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Ghanaian, Malik Abass, as a Canada-wide manhunt continues for two suspects. In an update issued on Thursday, November 19, 2026, police confirmed that they had obtained an extension of the authorisation under Section 110 of Canada’s Youth Criminal Justice Act, allowing them to release the identity and photographs of 17-year-old Cameron Marlor. The authorisation, which was due to expire, will now remain in force until Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at 12 noon. Police have also confirmed that a Canada-wide warrant has been issued for Marlor, who is from Toronto, on four charges: Second-degree murder. Attempted murder. Knowingly possessing a firearm without a licence. Possessing a loaded regulated firearm. A second suspect, 19-year-old Armani Callender, also from Toronto, is wanted under a Canada-wide warrant on the same four charges. The development expands police efforts to identify and locate the suspects as investigators continue their search and work to advance the homicide investigation. Read Also: 18-year-old Ghanaian shot in Canada identified as victim of Toronto’s 33rd homicide in 2026 Malik Abass, an 18-year-old from Mississauga, was killed on November 7, 2026, in the area of Rathburn Road and The East Mall in Toronto. Toronto Police have released photographs of the two suspects and are appealing to members of the public who may have information about their whereabouts to assist with the investigation. The killing of the young Ghanaian has drawn attention to the search for answers surrounding his death, with his family and the wider community awaiting developments as police intensify efforts to locate the two suspects. The manhunt remains ongoing.

items.title: Silicon Valley is Suffering From Model Collapse
items.description: For anyone living outside Northern California, a lot of the messages coming out of Silicon Valley feel like they’ve been sent from another planet. Last week, many of the industry’s top minds engaged in Olympic-level mental gymnastics as they defended the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs: We must excuse his dalliances with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, they argued, not just because Huang is absolutely necessary to the American economy, which is being propped up by AI investment, but because we are in a geopolitical superintelligence race with China. Then this week, Anthropic, the company most vocally obsessed with the existential risk of AI, went public in an effort to raise $90 billion so that it could speed up construction of the very same systems it’s warning us about. How do we explain this pattern of illogical behavior? Maybe it’s standard avarice: Shareholders stand to make unfathomable amounts of money from Nvidia and Anthropic stock, and, ultimately, cash rules everything around me. But many Anthropic employees seem uninterested in the money. Maybe it’s groupthink. Maybe it’s a religious-level belief in the abundance of a future in which humans have ushered in superintelligence. Or maybe it’s the cult of the founder and a messianic sense of grandeur—the conviction that only those who see the future first in San Francisco can help protect us from the scourge of disease, from the Chinese, or from ourselves. [ Read: ] A $5.7 trillion face-plant But watching the AI doomerism on X, the lead-up to Anthropic’s IPO, and the fallout from Huang’s resignation, I think there’s a better framework for understanding what we’re seeing. The degradation of logic, the inscrutable decision making, and the bizarre detachment from popular opinion all point to a dynamic that the AI industry calls model collapse. The term describes a type of digital inbreeding that can theoretically occur when AI models train off synthetic AI output. The most influential figures in AI now sound as if they, having marinated in the insular worlds of the Bay Area and X, are suffering from their own version of the phenomenon. Model collapse isn’t a perfect analogy. AI companies actually take pains to filter out AI slop when training their language models. But humans? Not so much. You might call it circular reasoning, but the overall takeaway is the same: The corporate leaders shaping our future seem stuck in their own world. A recent post on a popular AI blog captures this spirit well, comparing AI-company employees to people who are microdosing psychedelics. These individuals appear as if they are “in a chronically mildly altered state of mind,” the post argues. Maybe, the post suggests, this state of mind allows them to “see some things more clearly” about AI models and their progress and capabilities than those of us on the outside. The downside, of course, is some form of inebriation. This is a helpful framework through which to view a lot of what’s coming out of the Bay Area. But there’s also a compounding effect: All day, every day, this culture talks with itself, its participants training on a recursive loop of information about the world and what they are building. This information bubble is self-reinforcing, frequently illogical, and also alienating. The Silicon Valley discourse about recursive self improvement in AI offers the best example of this degraded, circular reasoning. RSI refers to the concept of AI models improving themselves without human intervention or supervision, which would improve AI capabilities exponentially, accelerating discoveries in different fields and increasing the likelihood that models show signs of superintelligence and become far better than humans at any task they pursue. The downside of RSI, according to individuals including the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, is that models “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.” Humans would be flying blind and thus would likely rely more heavily on AI systems to interpret what is happening inside other AI systems. This is already happening to varying degrees when AI companies train and test new models, but RSI would speed it up to the point that humans would have fully relinquished control. This prospect seems to terrify many of the people who are closest to the technology. “There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI. Please look up!” Anna Wang, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, wrote this fall. Yet companies keep racing toward RSI out of fear that someone less principled will get there first. Anthropic argues that pushing forward with an eye toward AI safety will create a virtuous cycle of innovation—a “race to the top.” But you could just as easily argue that these companies are plowing ahead to justify and pay for hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure investments. Or that they are so deeply locked in competition with other AI companies and open models in China that they’re behaving irrationally. This September, Amodei wrote an essay arguing for a multilateral slowdown of AI development, a process he dubbed “pacing the frontier.” Ten days later, Anthropic released its newest model. Roughly a month later, in its IPO filing, the company confessed that its call to pace the frontier “does not describe our own model development or release timelines.” Sometimes, you can see the model collapse happening at an individual level—and it looks like naked hypocrisy. In September, an Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon quit the company in order to argue that AI companies might kill us all. He offered a heartfelt and convincing case in favor of taking the risk of human extinction seriously. But then, when asked in an interview that surfaced this week whether he would donate his OpenAI shares, he seemed to laugh off the suggestion that doing so would make any difference. “I like the money, bro,” he told the audience. He has since agreed to donate his equity. Sigal Samuel, a writer who covers AI at Vox , has argued that at least some of this dynamic can be explained by a Silicon Valley culture steeped in effective altruism and rationalism. In this sphere, it’s not uncommon for adherents to justify huge risks using counterintuitive and dispassionate rationale. Some see this as a sophisticated form of argumentation, one that can eschew conventional morality (by risking rogue-AI swarm hacks or worse) for a greater purpose (achieving a technological utopia). Samuel argues that the hyperrational thinking deployed by these leaders is overly clever. “Commonsense morality is actually often commonsense for a reason,” she told me recently. “And that’s because it tracks intuitions. Usually, reasoning like ‘If you don’t want a doom machine, don’t build a doom machine’ tends to be good reasoning.” Some who have quit the AI companies in protest describe the internal cultures as nonsensical, even schizophrenic, in nature. David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s transparency reports as a safety lead, argued in this publication that the company, which speaks obsessively about safety, approached AI development “with unimpeded optimism about being able to solve problems as they arise,” leading it to adopt a trial-and-error approach that is no longer responsible, given the power of its models. Relentless optimism is a necessary component of technological achievement but, as Robinson suggests, it can veer into hubris. And so the Gordian knot grows ever tighter: Founders argue that humanity must accept enormous trade-offs for the benefit of a technological revolution. In exchange for curing cancer, one must be willing to risk the many-sided threat of gradual disempowerment, in the form of either mass job loss or a world where much of the cognitive work is performed by machines . Many of the people grinding away to usher in this future seem to lack humility or be unable to articulate whether the society they’re building toward is one that’s worth living in at all. At some point, their plainly stated claims can end up sounding, frankly, insane. Recently on X, an AI enthusiast argued that one possible positive end state for humans in an AI utopia would be that “we become the happy dogs” living in a world that “does not belong to them.” Musk has said that we might end up like a “pet Labrador if we’re lucky.” He has also argued that it is “unlikely” that humans will be in control in 10 years time. It all signals a certain irrational confidence in where the future is headed, and a disregard for how off-putting it all sounds. To prevent model collapse, AI companies don’t just add more data to training sets; they add higher-quality information from a diverse array of sources. The dynamic, according to some research , is not an evenly distributed phenomenon, meaning that it appears in specific areas of a model where there are weak points in the training data. A natural fix is to identify the blind spots or shallow areas and bolster them with better data. If Silicon Valley followed this example, perhaps what they would find is an enormous political blind spot. A June survey of Americans by the Pew Research Center showed that just 9 percent of respondents were more excited than concerned about AI, while 52 percent were more concerned than excited. In an exit poll from the recent midterm elections, 56 percent of voters responded that AI and data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in how they had voted. A recent survey of 1,000 young Americans suggested that few of them trust tech CEOs to act responsibly with AI. Yet many voices in Silicon Valley seem either disconnected from this reality or spiteful of it, accusing anti–data center voters of destroying America’s path to prosperity. As the fallout from the Nvidia scandal shows, Silicon Valley’s disconnect goes beyond just the general public; the venture capitalists arguing for Huang’s reinstatement seem to miss or simply not care about the bipartisan anger in Washington over Huang’s clearly reckless behavior. In an industry that has thoroughly embraced civilizational risk, the notion of the replaceable founder seems to be the true existential threat to the tech elite. Tech executives are failing at politics for the same reason they’re struggling among regular Americans: They’ve been so monomaniacally focused on winning the AI race that they’ve ignored everything else, including the need to build consensus or even a baseline of enthusiasm for their plans. That may be why the midterm shift away from MAGA took them by surprise. Maybe it’s because they believe that nobody, outside of the AI companies, is qualified or intelligent enough to judge their work, making them both perpetually unaccountable and correct in every argument. Perhaps it is because they believe that the technology is so self-evidently powerful that a public consensus is irrelevant. That could prove to be true, but in the interim, their rhetoric comes off as incomprehensible, frequently condescending, and too often frantic. At some point, the behaviors that signal a model collapse can also resemble those of a gambler on a bender. One day’s ecstasy over abundant superintelligence turns into the next day’s dire warnings about the future. Half of Silicon Valley appears to be arguing that AI progress is unstoppable—that human loss of control (or life ) within the next year seems inevitable; the other half seems to suggest that the entire fate of both AI progress and the economy hinges on one man in a leather jacket who sells chips. Regardless, the only way out is through, so you go harder and faster—anything to increase your odds. The AI industry, after all, is built on a historic bet: of marshaling as much human knowledge and capital as possible to conjure an alien intelligence greater than our own. Everything we’ve seen from Silicon Valley’s leaders in recent months—the legitimate safety fears, the people willing to cast all morality aside to defend Huang—is the result of this bet. The model-collapse behavior is its own form of recursive self-destruction: AI companies are building the very thing they fear; safety obsessives are alienating themselves from the public who could help them tackle an extraordinary collective-action problem. This is what happens when the bet becomes so big—when the industry is so full of financial, geopolitical, and existential risk—that it creates its own warped logic. It transforms human innovation from a worthy ambition to an inexorable force and, finally, into something akin to a hostage situation. To stop now, Silcon Valley’s leaders argue, would mean losing not merely the future, but also the present. We’re committed to whatever happens next; nothing is more important than driving forward, and no price is too steep. This is the lie the gambler tells himself. But how can we accept the premise when the logic behind it is degraded? I don’t doubt the power or even the potential of what many in Silicon Valley are building. But this is an industry that is asking for an unprecedented level of trust—trust it has neither earned nor seems all that interested in cultivating. At least for now, humans still have a right to self-determination and are under no obligation to submit to an ideology that might remove our agency without our consent. No vision of the future, no matter how well capitalized it is, is inevitable. Silicon Valley must widen the aperture. Its leaders must broaden the conversation around what this future might look like, what we will value, and how to keep it human.

items.title: Ouagadougou : La BMCRF traque les restaurants et koisque qui utilisent le gaz butane subventionné
items.description: À l’approche de la saison fraîche, la Brigade mobile de contrôle économique et de répression des fraudes (BMCRF) intensifie ses opérations contre l’utilisation du gaz butane subventionné à des fins commerciales. Les restaurants et les kiosques sont particulièrement ciblés afin de préserver l’approvisionnement des ménages. La Brigade mobile de contrôle économique et de répression des fraudes (BMCRF) renforce la lutte contre le détournement du gaz butane subventionné au Burkina Faso. Le jeudi 19 novembre 2026, ses équipes ont mené des opérations de contrôle dans des restaurants et des kiosques à Ouagadougou pour traquer les usages non conformes de cette ressource destinée prioritairement aux ménages. Cette offensive intervient à l’approche de la saison fraîche, période durant laquelle la demande en gaz domestique connaît une hausse. Selon la BMCRF, l’utilisation des bouteilles subventionnées dans les activités commerciales risque de perturber l’approvisionnement des ménages et de favoriser des tensions sur le marché. Des bouteilles de 1 à 12,5 kg réservées aux ménages La réglementation en vigueur établit une distinction entre les formats de bouteilles selon leur destination. Les bouteilles de gaz butane de 1 à 12,5 kg, bénéficiant de la subvention de l’État, sont exclusivement réservées aux besoins domestiques. En revanche, les bouteilles de 15 kg et plus, non subventionnées, sont destinées aux activités commerciales, notamment la restauration. À travers ces contrôles, la BMCRF entend faire respecter cette réglementation, limiter les détournements et garantir une meilleure disponibilité du gaz subventionné pour les familles. Transporteurs et revendeurs également dans le viseur La Brigade annonce par ailleurs un renforcement des contrôles sur l’ensemble de la chaîne de distribution. Les transporteurs ainsi que les revendeurs informels sont également concernés par cette opération de surveillance. La BMCRF invite les populations à signaler toute pratique suspecte ou tout manquement à la réglementation à travers ses numéros verts : 80 00 11 84 / 80 00 11 85 / 80 00 11 86. L’article Ouagadougou : La BMCRF traque les restaurants et koisque qui utilisent le gaz butane subventionné est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .
